newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German force preparing for Bosnia - Kinkel.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German force preparing for Bosnia - Kinkel.

text.p: Germany and France have made advanced preparations for a joint peacekeeping force in Bosnia once the mandate of the current NATO-led IFOR peace force expires, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Thursday.
"Planning for that is already quite far advanced," Kinkel told a news conference during a state visit to France by German President Roman Herzog.

He said the force would require a United Nations mandate and he assumed the German cabinet and parliament would approve the first such direct use of German troops in a potential combat role outside the NATO area since World War Two.
The German army has so far had only a support role within the peace Implementation Force (IFOR), with German troops based in neighbouring Croatia and running supply convoys into Bosnia.

"Once there is a U.N. mandate and a decision by the cabinet and parliament, which I assume will be positive, we would take part in a post-IFOR force in Bosnia in close Franco-German coordination and military integration of our forces," he said.
Kinkel did not say which units would participate in such a force, in which diplomats expect the United States to agree to participate once the November 5 presidential election is over.
But diplomats said the 5,000-strong Franco-German brigade, a bilingual force based in Muelheim in southwestern Germany, was earmarked for the assignment.

That would be politically symbolic, since the brigade was the first joint force established by the two former enemies and is the nucleus of a European army corps, which Belgium, Spain and Luxembourg have joined.
However it could be politically sensitive, since it the unit's rank and file are conscripts. France has so far sent only professional soldiers or conscript volunteers to ex-Yugoslavia.
In Brussels, NATO nations formally instructed the military on Wednesday to start working on a possible new peace force for Bosnia when IFOR's mandate expires at the end of December.
The alliance's military planners were asked to work on a range of options from stopping a fresh outbreak of fighting to wide-ranging support for civilian reconstruction efforts.
Kinkel welcomed what he called France's decision to return fully to NATO's military wing and cited cooperation on Bosnia as an example of increasing Franco-German defence integration.
He said Bonn fully backed French demand that the United States yield NATO's southern command, based in Naples, Italy, to a European officer.
Washington has refused, saying it will not give up the key post because it also controls the nuclear-armed U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean.

Herzog and Kinkel both thanked President Jacques Chirac for reaffirming France's support for giving Germany a permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council, which he spelled out in a dinner speech on Wednesday night.

Kinkel said there was broad agreement at the United Nations on adding Germany and Japan to the five existing permanent members -- the United States, Russia, France, Britain and China -- but differences remained on how Asia, Latin America and Africa should be represented on the Security Council.
He forecast that a solution would eventually be reached where they had a rotating representation.
